name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_NOMENCLATURE_MCQ_Q01 - Common trivial names and systematic IUPAC names

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Common Name) List II (IUPAC Name)
(A) Anisole (I) 2,2-Dimethylpropane
(B) Acetophenone (II) Methoxybenzene
(C) Formic acid (III) Methanoic acid
(D) Neopentane (IV) 1-Phenylethan-1-one

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Many common organic compounds have historical trivial names that are retained or related systematically to their standard IUPAC nomenclature based on their parent hydrocarbon chain and principal functional groups.

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- Anisole is the trivial name for methyl phenyl ether, having the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3}\). Under the IUPAC system, it is designated as methoxybenzene.
- Acetophenone consists of a phenyl group and a methyl group bonded to a carbonyl carbon, represented as \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\). Its systematic IUPAC name is 1-phenylethan-1-one (or acetophenone, which is also retained by IUPAC).
- Formic acid is the simplest carboxylic acid, \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\), traditionally obtained by the destructive distillation of red ants (Latin: formica). In systematic IUPAC nomenclature, the one-carbon carboxylic acid is named methanoic acid.
- Neopentane is the common name for the branched isomer of pentane with a quaternary central carbon atom, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_4C}\). The longest continuous carbon chain has three carbons with two methyl substituents at C-2, giving the systematic IUPAC name 2,2-dimethylpropane.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Anisole corresponds to methoxybenzene.
- Acetophenone corresponds to 1-phenylethan-1-one.
- Formic acid corresponds to methanoic acid.
- Neopentane corresponds to 2,2-dimethylpropane.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_MOLECULAR_MODELS_MCQ_Q02 - Characteristics and representations of molecular models

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Molecular Model) List II (Structural Feature / Description)
(A) Framework model (I) Displays relative sizes of each atom based on its van der Waals radius without showing explicit bonds
(B) Ball-and-stick model (I) Emphasizes the skeletal framework and bonds while neglecting the sizes of individual atoms
(C) Ball-and-spring model (III) Employs rigid balls to represent atoms and cylindrical sticks to indicate covalent bonds
(D) Space-filling model (IV) Employs flexible connectors suited to represent strained rings or multiple bonds

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Three-dimensional representations of molecules in chemistry are constructed using specific physical model types, each highlighting distinct stereochemical and spatial properties.

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- The framework model emphasizes the overall pattern of chemical bonds and skeletal geometry between atoms while largely omitting the physical volume or relative sizes of the atoms themselves.
- The ball-and-stick model depicts individual atoms as spherical balls of varying sizes or colours and covalent single bonds as rigid wooden or plastic cylindrical sticks, clearly illustrating bond angles and spatial orientation.
- The ball-and-spring model substitutes flexible metallic or plastic springs in place of rigid sticks to depict double bonds, triple bonds, or strained ring geometries where parallel or bent bonds are required.
- The space-filling model conveys realistic steric bulk and molecular envelope by packing spherically truncated atoms touching one another, scaled according to their respective van der Waals radii, without showing explicit sticks or springs for bonds.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Framework model corresponds to emphasizing the skeletal framework and bonds while neglecting the sizes of individual atoms.
- Ball-and-stick model corresponds to employing rigid balls to represent atoms and cylindrical sticks to indicate covalent bonds.
- Ball-and-spring model corresponds to employing flexible connectors suited to represent strained rings or multiple bonds.
- Space-filling model corresponds to displaying relative sizes of each atom based on its van der Waals radius without showing explicit bonds.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_CLASSIFICATION_MCQ_Q03 - Classification of organic ring systems and aromaticity

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Compound) List II (Structural Class)
(A) Tetrahydrofuran (I) Benzenoid aromatic compound
(B) Tropone (II) Alicyclic heterocyclic compound
(C) Pyridine (III) Non-benzenoid aromatic compound
(D) Naphthalene (IV) Heterocyclic aromatic compound

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Organic compounds are classified based on the nature of their carbon skeleton into acyclic and cyclic systems. Cyclic compounds are further subdivided into homocyclic (alicyclic and aromatic) and heterocyclic (alicyclic and aromatic). Aromatic compounds can contain isolated or fused benzene rings (benzenoid) or possess aromatic stability without a benzene ring (non-benzenoid).

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- Tetrahydrofuran (THF) is a saturated five-membered cyclic ether containing four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom in the ring. Because it lacks an aromatic \(\pi\)-electron system and resembles an aliphatic open-chain ether in reactivity, it is categorized as an alicyclic heterocyclic compound.
- Tropone (cyclohepta-2,4,6-trien-1-one) is a seven-membered planar conjugated carbocyclic ketone. The dipolar resonance contributor possesses a six-\(\pi\)-electron tropylium cation ring, imparting distinct aromatic stability without containing a six-membered benzene nucleus. Hence, it is a non-benzenoid aromatic compound.
- Pyridine is a six-membered aromatic ring containing five carbon atoms and one nitrogen heteroatom, exhibiting aromaticity via six delocalised \(\pi\)-electrons. Because the ring contains a non-carbon heteroatom, it is a heterocyclic aromatic compound.
- Naphthalene consists of two fused benzene rings sharing a common pair of adjacent carbons, containing a fully conjugated \(10\,\pi\)-electron system that obeys Hückel's rule (\(4n+2\), with \(n=2\)). It is a classic benzenoid aromatic compound.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Tetrahydrofuran corresponds to alicyclic heterocyclic compound.
- Tropone corresponds to non-benzenoid aromatic compound.
- Pyridine corresponds to heterocyclic aromatic compound.
- Naphthalene corresponds to benzenoid aromatic compound.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_ISOMERISM_MCQ_Q04 - Classification of pairs of structural isomers

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Pair of Compounds) List II (Type of Structural Isomerism)
(A) Pentane and 2,2-Dimethylpropane (I) Metamerism
(B) Propan-1-ol and Propan-2-ol (II) Chain isomerism
(C) Propanone and Propanal (III) Functional group isomerism
(D) Methoxypropane and Ethoxyethane (IV) Position isomerism

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Structural isomers possess the same molecular formula but differ in connectivity, arrangement of carbon skeletons, position of functional groups, nature of functional groups, or distribution of alkyl groups on polyvalent heteroatoms.

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- Pentane, \(\mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_3CH_3}\), and 2,2-dimethylpropane, \(\mathrm{C(CH_3)_4}\), share the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\) but have different carbon chain skeletons (a five-carbon unbranched chain versus a three-carbon branched chain). They are chain isomers.
- Propan-1-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\), and propan-2-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3}\), both possess the identical three-carbon chain and the hydroxyl functional group (\(\mathrm{-OH}\)), but the hydroxyl group is attached to C-1 in the first compound and to C-2 in the second. They are position isomers.
- Propanone, \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\), and propanal, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}\), share the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_6O}\), but the former is an aliphatic ketone containing a carbonyl group bounded by two carbons, whereas the latter is an aldehyde containing an aldo group. They are functional group isomers.
- Methoxypropane, \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-CH_2CH_2CH_3}\), and ethoxyethane, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-O-CH_2CH_3}\), share the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\) and contain the same bivalent ether functional group (\(\mathrm{-O-}\)), but differ in the unequal distribution of alkyl groups attached to the oxygen atom (methyl/propyl versus ethyl/ethyl). They are metamers.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane correspond to chain isomerism.
- Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol correspond to position isomerism.
- Propanone and propanal correspond to functional group isomerism.
- Methoxypropane and ethoxyethane correspond to metamerism.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_REACTION_INTERMEDIATES_MCQ_Q05 - Electronic structure and characteristics of reactive intermediates

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Intermediate / Reagent) List II (Structural Feature / Character)
(A) Methyl carbocation (I) Neutral species with seven valence electrons containing an unpaired electron
(B) Methyl carbanion (II) Trigonal planar species with \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon and an empty \(2p\) orbital
(C) Methyl free radical (III) Electron-seeking chemical species that accepts an electron pair from a substrate
(D) Electrophile (IV) Negatively charged species with eight valence electrons and pyramidal geometry

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Heterolytic and homolytic cleavage of covalent bonds generate transient reactive intermediates—carbocations, carbanions, and carbon free radicals—which exhibit distinctive valence electronic configurations, hybridisation states, and molecular geometries.

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- A methyl carbocation, \(\mathrm{\overset{+}{C}H_3}\), is formed by heterolytic cleavage where the leaving group departs with the bonding pair. The positively charged carbon has six valence electrons, is \(sp^2\) hybridised, adopts a trigonal planar geometry, and possesses a vacant unhybridised \(2p\) orbital perpendicular to the molecular plane.
- A methyl carbanion, \(\mathrm{:\overset{-}{C}H_3}\), is formed by heterolysis where the carbon atom retains the bonding electron pair. The central carbon has eight valence electrons (an octet including one non-bonding lone pair), is \(sp^3\) hybridised, and adopts a pyramidal (distorted tetrahedral) geometry.
- A methyl free radical, \(\mathrm{\overset{\bullet}{C}H_3}\), is generated by homolytic bond fission where each fragment retains one electron of the shared pair. The resulting neutral carbon has seven valence electrons, containing a single unpaired electron.
- An electrophile is an electron-deficient reagent ("electron-loving") that accepts an electron pair from an electron-rich substrate during a reaction.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Methyl carbocation corresponds to trigonal planar species with \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon and an empty \(2p\) orbital.
- Methyl carbanion corresponds to negatively charged species with eight valence electrons and pyramidal geometry.
- Methyl free radical corresponds to neutral species with seven valence electrons containing an unpaired electron.
- Electrophile corresponds to electron-seeking chemical species that accepts an electron pair from a substrate.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_ELECTRONIC_EFFECTS_MCQ_Q06 - Fundamental electronic displacement effects in organic molecules

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Electronic Effect) List II (Defining Characteristics)
(A) Inductive effect (I) Temporary complete transfer of a shared pair of \(\pi\)-electrons on demand of an attacking reagent
(B) Electromeric effect (II) Permanent polarisation along \(\sigma\)-bonds caused by electronegativity differences, diminishing rapidly with distance
(C) Resonance effect (III) Delocalisation of \(\sigma\)-electrons of a \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond into an adjacent empty or partially filled \(p\) orbital
(D) Hyperconjugation (IV) Permanent polarity produced by interaction of two \(\pi\)-bonds or between a \(\pi\)-bond and a lone pair on an adjacent atom

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Reactivity and physical properties of organic molecules are governed by electronic displacements, which can be permanent ground-state phenomena (inductive, resonance, and hyperconjugation) or temporary effects induced by an attacking reagent (electromeric effect).

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- The inductive effect is a permanent displacement of \(\sigma\)-electrons along a carbon chain arising from electronegativity differences between bonded atoms. The polarisation decreases sharply with increasing distance and becomes virtually negligible beyond three carbon atoms.
- The electromeric effect is a purely temporary phenomenon operating in unsaturated compounds containing multiple bonds, where the complete transfer of a shared pair of \(\pi\)-electrons to one of the atoms takes place only when an attacking reagent demands it, vanishing once the reagent is removed.
- The resonance (mesomeric) effect is a permanent polarity generated in a conjugated system by the interaction of two \(\pi\)-bonds or between a \(\pi\)-bond and a lone pair of electrons present on an adjacent conjugated atom, represented via canonical structures.
- Hyperconjugation involves delocalisation of \(\sigma\)-electrons of an \(\alpha\text{-}\mathrm{C-H}\) bond into an adjacent vacant or partially filled \(p\) orbital or into a \(\pi\) molecular orbital, frequently termed no-bond resonance or the Baker-Nathan effect.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Inductive effect corresponds to permanent polarisation along \(\sigma\)-bonds caused by electronegativity differences, diminishing rapidly with distance.
- Electromeric effect corresponds to temporary complete transfer of a shared pair of \(\pi\)-electrons on demand of an attacking reagent.
- Resonance effect corresponds to permanent polarity produced by interaction of two \(\pi\)-bonds or between a \(\pi\)-bond and a lone pair on an adjacent atom.
- Hyperconjugation corresponds to delocalisation of \(\sigma\)-electrons of a \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond into an adjacent empty or partially filled \(p\) orbital.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_PURIFICATION_MCQ_Q07 - Purification techniques applied to specific industrial and laboratory mixtures

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Mixture to be Separated) List II (Purification Method)
(A) Chloroform and Aniline (I) Steam distillation
(B) Crude oil fractions (II) Distillation under reduced pressure
(C) Glycerol from spent-lye (III) Simple distillation
(D) Aniline from an aniline-water mixture (IV) Fractional distillation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The choice of distillation method depends on volatility, boiling point differences, thermal stability, and mutual solubility with water.

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- Chloroform (b.p. \(334\text{ K}\)) and aniline (b.p. \(457\text{ K}\)) have a large boiling point difference of \(123\text{ K}\). Liquids that boil without decomposition and have sufficiently wide boiling point differences (\(>25\text{ K}\)) are cleanly separated by simple distillation.
- Crude oil contains complex mixtures of liquid hydrocarbons with closely spaced boiling points. When boiling point differences are small, separation is achieved using a fractionating column via fractional distillation.
- Glycerol has a very high boiling point (\(563\text{ K}\)) and decomposes at or below its normal boiling point. In the soap industry, it is separated from spent-lye by distillation under reduced pressure (vacuum distillation), enabling it to boil at a much lower temperature without thermal degradation.
- Aniline is practically immiscible with water, volatile in steam, and possesses a significant partial vapor pressure at \(373\text{ K}\). Aniline from an aniline-water mixture is separated using steam distillation, which distills the mixture at a total pressure equal to atmospheric pressure at a temperature below \(373\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Chloroform and aniline corresponds to simple distillation.
- Crude oil fractions corresponds to fractional distillation.
- Glycerol from spent-lye corresponds to distillation under reduced pressure.
- Aniline from an aniline-water mixture corresponds to steam distillation.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_QUALITATIVE_ANALYSIS_MCQ_Q08 - Observations and products in Lassaignes elemental tests

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Qualitative Detection Test) List II (Observation / Reaction Product)
(A) Detection of nitrogen in Lassaigne's extract (I) Blood red colouration due to \([\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{SCN})]^{2+}\)
(B) Detection of sulphur using lead acetate (II) Prussian blue precipitate/colouration of \(\mathrm{Fe}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]_3\cdot x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)
(C) Detection of sulphur using sodium nitroprusside (III) Black precipitate of \(\mathrm{PbS}\)
(D) Simultaneous detection of nitrogen and sulphur (IV) Violet colouration due to \([\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_5\mathrm{NOS}]^{4-}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Lassaigne's test, organic compounds are fused with metallic sodium to convert covalently bonded heteroatoms (nitrogen, sulphur, halogens) into water-soluble ionic salts: \(\mathrm{NaCN}\), \(\mathrm{Na_2S}\), and \(\mathrm{NaSCN}\), which are subsequently identified via characteristic precipitation or complexation reactions.

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- When nitrogen alone is present, sodium fusion produces \(\mathrm{NaCN}\). Boiling with iron(II) sulphate (\(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\)) forms sodium hexacyanoferrate(II). Upon acidification with concentrated sulphuric acid, \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), which reacts with hexacyanoferrate(II) to yield a Prussian blue complex, iron(III) hexacyanoferrate(II), \(\mathrm{Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3\cdot xH_2O}\).
- When sulphur is present, sodium fusion produces \(\mathrm{Na_2S}\). Acidifying the extract with acetic acid followed by the addition of lead acetate solution produces a black precipitate of lead sulphide, \(\mathrm{PbS}\).
- Sulphur in the sodium fusion extract (\(\mathrm{Na_2S}\)) also reacts with freshly prepared aqueous sodium nitroprusside, \(\mathrm{Na_2[Fe(CN)_5NO]}\), yielding an intense violet colouration due to the formation of the complex ion \([\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_5\mathrm{NOS}]^{4-}\).
- When both nitrogen and sulphur are simultaneously present and sodium is not in large excess, sodium thiocyanate (\(\mathrm{NaSCN}\)) is formed. Upon adding \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) ions (from \(\mathrm{FeCl_3}\)), a characteristic blood red colouration appears due to the formation of \([\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{SCN})]^{2+}\) (ferric thiocyanate).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Detection of nitrogen in Lassaigne's extract corresponds to Prussian blue precipitate/colouration of \(\mathrm{Fe}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]_3\cdot x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).
- Detection of sulphur using lead acetate corresponds to black precipitate of \(\mathrm{PbS}\).
- Detection of sulphur using sodium nitroprusside corresponds to violet colouration due to \([\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_5\mathrm{NOS}]^{4-}\).
- Simultaneous detection of nitrogen and sulphur corresponds to blood red colouration due to \([\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{SCN})]^{2+}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_QUANTITATIVE_ANALYSIS_MCQ_Q09 - Chemical principles of quantitative estimation methods

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Quantitative Method) List II (Working Chemical Principle)
(A) Dumas method for nitrogen (I) Digestion with concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) to form \((\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), followed by distillation of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) into standard acid
(B) Kjeldahl's method for nitrogen (II) Combustion with \(\mathrm{CuO}\) in a \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) atmosphere, reduction of nitrogen oxides, and collecting \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gas over aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\)
(C) Carius method for halogens (III) Heating with fuming \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) and \(\mathrm{BaCl}_2\) in a sealed tube to precipitate and weigh \(\mathrm{BaSO}_4\)
(D) Carius method for sulphur (IV) Heating with fuming \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) in the presence of \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\) in a sealed tube to weigh \(\mathrm{AgX}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Quantitative elemental analysis involves stoichiometric conversion of elements present in organic compounds into measurable elemental gases, insoluble precipitates, or standard titratable solutions.

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- In Dumas method, a known mass of the nitrogenous compound is heated with copper(II) oxide in an atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\). Any oxides of nitrogen formed are passed over a heated copper spiral to reduce them to elemental nitrogen. The gaseous mixture is transferred into a nitrometer containing concentrated \(\mathrm{KOH}\) solution, which absorbs \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), allowing the dry volume of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gas to be measured.
- In Kjeldahl's method, the compound is digested with concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) (in the presence of \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) catalyst and \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) to raise the boiling point). Nitrogen is quantitatively converted to ammonium sulphate, \((\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{SO_4}\). Boiling the digested mixture with excess \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) releases ammonia gas (\(\mathrm{NH_3}\)), which is absorbed in a known excess volume of standard acid and determined by back-titration.
- In the Carius method for halogens, the compound is heated with fuming nitric acid (\(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)) in the presence of silver nitrate (\(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\)) inside a sealed heavy-walled glass Carius tube. The halogen is precipitated as silver halide (\(\mathrm{AgX}\)), which is filtered, washed, dried, and weighed.
- In the Carius method for sulphur, the organic compound is heated with fuming \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) in a sealed Carius tube, oxidising sulphur to sulphuric acid. Barium chloride solution (\(\mathrm{BaCl_2}\)) is added to precipitate barium sulphate (\(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\)), which is washed, ignited, and weighed.

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Dumas method for nitrogen corresponds to combustion with \(\mathrm{CuO}\) in a \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) atmosphere, reduction of nitrogen oxides, and collecting \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gas over aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\).
- Kjeldahl's method for nitrogen corresponds to digestion with concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) to form \((\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), followed by distillation of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) into standard acid.
- Carius method for halogens corresponds to heating with fuming \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) in the presence of \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\) in a sealed tube to weigh \(\mathrm{AgX}\).
- Carius method for sulphur corresponds to heating with fuming \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) and \(\mathrm{BaCl}_2\) in a sealed tube to precipitate and weigh \(\mathrm{BaSO}_4\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ORGANIC_REAGENTS_ANALYSIS_MCQ_Q10 - Chemical reagents and their specific analytical detection functions

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Reagent / Absorbing Agent) List II (Specific Role / Analytical Detection)
(A) Ninhydrin spray reagent (I) Absorption of acidic \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) gas during quantitative carbon estimation or Dumas method
(B) Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate (II) Visualisation of colourless amino acid spots on thin layer or paper chromatograms
(C) Ammonium molybdate in boiling \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) (III) Qualitative detection of water (hydrogen) formed during combustion by turning blue
(D) Concentrated potassium hydroxide solution (IV) Qualitative detection of phosphorus by formation of a canary yellow precipitate

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Qualitative, quantitative, and chromatographic analyses rely on specific chemical reagents and selective absorbents that produce unambiguous colour changes, precipitates, or chemical absorptions.

Step 2: Analysis of List I entries
- Ninhydrin spray solution is a specialised developing/visualising reagent used in thin-layer and paper chromatography to detect colourless amino acids and proteins, yielding a characteristic purple/violet Ruhemann's purple product upon reaction.
- Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate (\(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\)) is a white hygroscopic powder used in the Liebig combustion tube apparatus to detect water vapour generated from the oxidation of hydrogen present in the organic compound. As it hydrates to form \(\mathrm{CuSO_4\cdot 5H_2O}\), its colour distinctly changes from white to blue.
- Ammonium molybdate reagent in the presence of concentrated nitric acid is used to detect phosphorus. When the sodium peroxide fusion product (\(\mathrm{Na_3PO_4}\)) is boiled with nitric acid and treated with ammonium molybdate, \(\mathrm{(NH_4)_2MoO_4}\), it yields a characteristic canary yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate, \(\mathrm{(NH_4)_3PO_4\cdot 12MoO_3}\).
- Concentrated aqueous potassium hydroxide solution (\(\mathrm{KOH}\)) is strongly alkaline and is specifically employed in Dumas nitrometers and Liebig combustion bulb sets to selectively absorb acidic carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)) gas according to \(2\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
- Ninhydrin spray reagent corresponds to visualisation of colourless amino acid spots on thin layer or paper chromatograms.
- Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate corresponds to qualitative detection of water (hydrogen) formed during combustion by turning blue.
- Ammonium molybdate in boiling \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) corresponds to qualitative detection of phosphorus by formation of a canary yellow precipitate.
- Concentrated potassium hydroxide solution corresponds to absorption of acidic \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) gas during quantitative carbon estimation or Dumas method.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.
